tier_reason: README Benchmark section shows pcl_gicp and pcl_ndt against fgicp/vgicp variants on a Core i9-9900K + RTX 2080 Ti, produced by the public src/align.cpp; CMakeLists.txt forces CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release plus OpenMP, but the compiler is never named, so it cannot be A and stays first-party C.

corrections.caveats: Tier would be A except that the compiler is never named and the flags come only from the CMake Release default plus OpenMP, so it stays C (own-repo benchmark with partial methodology). Benchmark code is public (src/align.cpp) but the README shows a single scan pair (data/251370668.pcd vs 251371071.pcd) on one machine. Most of the speedup comes from multithreading and GPU use against PCL's default single-threaded GICP/NDT: fgicp_mt and vgicp_mt both run with omp_get_max_threads() (FastGICP's constructor default; align.cpp leaves setNumThreads(8) commented out), and the thread count actually used on the 8-core/16-thread i9-9900K is not printed. Single-threaded fgicp_st is only about 1.15x faster than pcl_gicp. The PCL version is not stated; iteration and convergence settings are each class's defaults and were not verified to be identical; pcl_ndt reaches a worse fitness (0.2296) than the GICP variants (about 0.204), so it is a different algorithm rather than a like-for-like baseline. align.cpp also prints ndt_cuda rows that the README output omits. The ICRA 2021 VGICP paper was not opened. The README badges and install commands still point to SMRT-AIST/fast_gicp (the copyright holder), and the README now announces small_gicp (already listed as koide3/small_gicp) as the faster successor library. Last commit 2025-04-24 (over 12 months).

notes: Benchmark table, hardware line and BSD-3-Clause license verified from the README, LICENSE, CMakeLists.txt and src/align.cpp; github.com page shows 1.7k stars, 374 forks, not archived, not a fork; last commit 2025-04-24 (stale). Separate project from the already-listed successor koide3/small_gicp, so not a duplicate, but worth cross-linking.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Performance Comparison page (seconds; 3 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i5; iOverlay Rust v1.9.0 multithreading on/off, iOverlay Swift v1.13.0, Clipper2 C++ v1.4.0, Boost C++ 1.86.0). Checkerboard test, 8,384,513 squares: Rust mt on 33.742 s, Rust mt off 38.640 s, Clipper2 644.338 s, about 19.1x (mt on) and 16.7x (mt off) faster (derived from page data); at 2,095,105 squares 7.94 s / 9.29 s versus 73.31 s. Not Overlap, 8,384,513 squares: 9.60 s / 13.51 s versus 167.97 s (17.5x / 12.4x, derived). Windows, 8,388,608: 12.06 s / 15.48 s versus 265.39 s (22.0x / 17.1x, derived). Spiral, 1,048,576: 3.23 s / 3.19 s versus 259.87 s (about 80x, derived). Lines Net 4096: 7.70 s / 7.51 s versus 45.93 s (about 6x, derived). Nested Squares 65,536: 2.20 s / 4.03 s versus 3502.23 s for Clipper2. Clipper2 is as fast or faster on small inputs (for example Checkerboard 481 squares 1.017 ms versus 1.117 ms; Lines Net up to 256; Spiral up to 1024). Boost is far slower where it ran (Checkerboard 32,513 squares 412.6 s versus 0.092 s for Rust mt off) and has no results for the largest sizes. The repo README chart separately reports iOverlay-internal relative times only (Apple M4, 24 GB, geometric mean, i32 multithreading off = 1.00x: i16 off 0.92x, i64 off 1.30x, i16 on 0.85x, i32 on 0.86x, i64 on 1.08x).

corrections.caveats: Rust library (C++ is only the baseline). The comparison page lives on ishape-rust.github.io, which is EGRESS_BLOCKED; its numbers were read from the page's checked-in mdBook output at iShape-Rust/iShape-js docs/overlay/performance/performance.html via raw.githubusercontent.com. First-party benchmark by the iOverlay author: the CPU is described only as '3 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i5', no compiler or toolchain is named, BoostApp sets no CMake build type, and ClipperApp also carries a cmake-build-debug directory, so it is not established that every baseline ran an optimised build (build.sh does request Release for Clipper2). Clipper2 runs single-threaded; the 'mt on' column uses iOverlay's multithreading, while 'mt off' is the fair single-thread comparison (16.7x on the largest checkerboard). The measured versions are old: iOverlay Rust v1.9.0 (crates.io 2024-11-20) versus current 9.0.0, and Clipper2 v1.4.0; the perf app now builds iOverlay from a local path, so the published table may not match the code in the repo today. Clipper2 is equal or faster on small inputs and on Lines Net/Spiral up to about a thousand elements; the large factors come from asymptotic behaviour on adversarial synthetic grids, not typical GIS data. Boost results stop at mid sizes. The repo README chart itself shows only internal engine variants (multithreading cuts relative time by about 8 to 17 percent on average). OpenROAD discussion #5864 (opened by the search agent, written by the iOverlay author) separately claims xOverlay is 10-20x faster than Boost.Polygon in most benchmarks; not verified here.

corrections.caveats: Numbers are from a search-result snippet only: arxiv.org, drops.dagstuhl.de, par.nsf.gov, www.cs.ucr.edu and www.cs.umd.edu were all EGRESS_BLOCKED (www.cs.ucr.edu re-checked by the verifier), so benchmark_url was NOT opened and the CPU model, compiler, baseline versions and point types are unknown. The repo itself carries no CGAL or Qhull comparison: benchmark/hull3d_bench.cpp times only serialQuick_* versus pseudo_* on 10M synthetic sets and scanned models, with maxThreads = 72. The README cites only the PPoPP 2022 poster and the GeoGraph paper, while the lead named ESA 2022; the ESA title match came from the search snippet. Parallel versus sequential baselines means unequal core counts; the 559x figure is against 'best existing sequential implementation', not CGAL. The original repo wangyiqiu/pargeo (12 stars) now points to ParAlg/ParGeo. Last commit 2022-09-12 (over 4 years, not archived).
